title: Prompt Shields
summary: Prompt Shields detects two attack families: user prompt attacks typed by the caller and document attacks hidden in content the model reads. It is a probabilistic classifier, one layer of a defence in depth.
useIf: Your model reads text you do not control: user input, retrieved documents, web pages, emails or tool output.
avoidIf: You expect it to be a complete defence: pair it with least privilege, Spotlighting where available and deterministic blocks on exfiltration paths.

explain.md: **User prompt attacks** (formerly jailbreak risk detection) try to override the system rules. The documented subtypes are changing system rules, conversation mockup, role-play and encoding. **Document attacks** (indirect attacks) hide instructions in content such as a retrieved page or an email: the subtypes include manipulated content, system access, information gathering, availability, fraud and malware, plus the four user-attack types. Prompt Shields has been GA since August 2024 [[r3]].

In Foundry guardrails the annotations carry `detected` and `filtered` booleans. In the standalone API you send one `userPrompt` and up to five `documents` and read `attackDetected`. The prompt limit is 10K characters, and Prompt Shields was tested on English only, so test other languages yourself [[r3]] [[r10]]. A top-12 retrieval therefore needs three calls, which you can run in parallel to protect latency.

**Spotlighting** is a separate, Azure preview feature for document attacks. It marks documents as lower trust by base64 encoding them. It is off by default, works with the Chat Completions API on models only (not agents), raises token counts and can push a long document over the input limit, and the model may mention base64 in answers [[r3]]. The Microsoft paper reports attack success falling from above 50 percent to below 2 percent on GPT-family models with minimal task impact [[r12]]. The MSRC defence in depth guidance combines prompt hardening, Spotlighting, Prompt Shields and deterministic blocking of exfiltration paths [[r11]].

whereToUse: RAG assistants that retrieve from wikis, tickets, shared drives or the web
Mail and calendar copilots where content comes from outside senders
Agents whose tools return web or file content
Public chat endpoints that face deliberate jailbreak attempts
Security reviews that map untrusted inputs to a scan point

use: Use the user-attack shield on every public prompt
Use the document-attack shield on retrieved chunks and tool responses when sources are not fully trusted
Use Spotlighting on models where preview is acceptable and token cost is fine
Combine with least-privilege tools and deterministic exfiltration blocks
avoid: Avoid relying on the shield alone: it is probabilistic and tested on English
Avoid Spotlighting for very long documents near the input limit
Avoid assuming Spotlighting protects agents: it is not supported for them
flips: Sources are a curated internal library: sample or relax document scanning, keep user-attack scanning
The workload is an agent rather than a model call: use the tool-response control instead of Spotlighting
Traffic is not English: build a local attack test set and add heuristics or classifiers

pitfalls.symptom: A planted instruction in a retrieved page changes the answer
pitfalls.cause: Only the user prompt was scanned
pitfalls.fix: Pass retrieved chunks as `documents` or enable the indirect attack control on tool responses

pitfalls.symptom: Long documents fail after enabling Spotlighting
pitfalls.cause: Base64 encoding raises token count past the input limit
pitfalls.fix: Shorten or chunk the documents, or skip Spotlighting for those requests

pitfalls.cause: The model sees encoded text and sometimes refers to it
pitfalls.fix: Instruct the model about the encoding and test output wording

pitfalls.cause: Prompt Shields was tested on English only
pitfalls.fix: Create a multilingual attack test set and add complementary controls

scenarios.title: Q&A over scraped web pages, no tools
scenarios.situation: An assistant answers from web pages the team crawls. It has no tools and returns 12 chunks per query. Latency budget is two seconds. Some pages may carry hidden instructions.
unknowns: Is the model in the Chat Completions API?
scenarios.question: What do you add for document attacks?

options.name: Scan chunks with the document shield in three parallel calls of up to five, plus an output guard
options.why: It matches the five-documents-per-call limit and parallelism keeps the added latency near one call.
options.tradeoff: Three calls per query and some false positives on benign pages.

options.name: Spotlighting only
options.why: Lowers attack success in the research and costs nothing per call.
options.tradeoff: Preview, adds base64 tokens and does not detect or report attacks.

options.name: Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore document instructions
options.why: It is the weakest control and attackers target exactly this.
options.tradeoff: Fine as one layer, never as the only layer.

flips.if: Pages come from a curated internal library
flips.then: Sample scanning or scan only new documents.
Skip Spotlighting for them and rely on shield scanning.

scenarios.takeaway: Scan what the model reads, in parallel batches that match the API limits.

scenarios.title: Foundry agent that calls a web-fetch tool
scenarios.situation: An agent in Foundry Agent Service fetches web pages through a tool and can write notes to a shared store. Preview features are acceptable for this pilot.
constraints: Foundry agent, not a bare model
Write access to a shared store
unknowns: Which domains may the tool fetch?
scenarios.question: Which controls do you rely on?

options.name: Indirect-attack control on tool responses, tool-call controls and a domain and write allow list
options.why: The document shield scans tool responses in Foundry, and tool-call checks plus allow lists limit damage if one slips.
options.tradeoff: Tool-level controls are preview, and allow lists restrict flexibility.

options.name: Prompt hardening plus output filtering
options.tradeoff: The side effect (writing to the store) happens before output is checked.

options.name: Spotlighting on the underlying model
options.why: Spotlighting is not supported for agents.
options.tradeoff: Right for plain model calls on the Chat Completions API.

flips.then: Implement tool response scanning and allow lists in your own code with the standalone API.

flips.if: The tool becomes read-only and the store is private

scenarios.takeaway: For agents, scan tool responses and limit what a hijacked agent can do.

quiz.q: The standalone Prompt Shields API accepts up to five documents per call. How many calls do you need to scan 12 retrieved chunks?
quiz.explain: 12 divided by 5 is 2.4, so 3 calls (5, 5 and 2). They can run in parallel, so added latency is about one call.

quiz.q: In Foundry, where are document (indirect) attacks scanned?
options: At user input and tool response
quiz.explain: User attacks are scanned at user input, and document attacks at user input and tool response. Output and embedding steps are not documented scan points for the shield, and tool call is a separate control.

quiz.q: Which are true about Spotlighting in Azure?
options: It can raise token counts and push long documents over the limit
quiz.explain: Spotlighting is off by default, base64 encodes documents and raises token counts. It is supported for models on the Chat Completions API, not agents.

flashcards.back: User prompt attacks (formerly jailbreak detection) and document attacks (indirect), the latter hidden in retrieved or tool-returned content.
One `userPrompt` and up to five `documents`. The response carries `attackDetected`. Prompt limit 10K characters.
Preview, base64 encodes documents, models only (not agents), raises tokens. Paper: attack success from above 50% to below 2%.
